title: How much cooler a city can be
lead: Trees, light roofs and planted roofs make a city less hot. Each bar shows how many degrees Celsius cooler, compared with an ordinary roof or a part of the city without green cover. Most figures are ranges or upper limits, because the result depends on climate, design and upkeep. All of them come from guidance by the United States Environmental Protection Agency.

tabs.main: How much cooler a city can be

cool-roof-indoor.name: Cool roofs
cool-roof-indoor.hook: In homes without air conditioning, a roof that reflects sunlight can lower the highest indoor temperature by 1.2 to 3.3 °C.
cool-roof-indoor.detail: A cool roof sends back more of the sun's energy than a dark roof, through a light coating, membrane, tile or shingle. In homes with air conditioning, the agency reports that it can cut peak cooling demand by 11 to 27 percent. In cold climates it can raise winter heating a little, which the agency says the summer savings usually outweigh.
cool-roof-indoor.caption: White stepped roofs of a house on the coast of Bermuda, photographed in May 1994.
cool-roof-indoor.credit: Photo: Acroterion, via Wikimedia Commons, licence Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0. Resized.
sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency: Using Cool Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands

urban-forest-cooling.name: Urban trees and parks
urban-forest-cooling.hook: A review of 308 studies found urban forests were on average 1.6 °C cooler than parts of the city without green cover.
urban-forest-cooling.detail: Trees cool the air in two ways: their shade keeps the sun off the ground, and their leaves give off water that takes heat from the air as it evaporates. The agency notes that neighbourhoods with fewer trees are hotter, and one study it cites found more people with lower incomes living in them.
urban-forest-cooling.caption: A brick street in Savannah, Georgia, in the United States, where large trees meet over the road.
urban-forest-cooling.credit: Photo: Michael Stokes, via Wikimedia Commons, licence Creative Commons Attribution 2.0. Resized.
sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency: Benefits of Trees and Vegetation

green-roof-air.name: Green roofs, air nearby
green-roof-air.hook: A planted roof can cool the air around it by up to 11 °C, or 20 °F, the agency reports.
green-roof-air.detail: A green roof is a layer of plants and growing soil on top of a waterproof layer. The plants shade the roof and give off water, which draws heat from the air. The agency also reports that green roofs can cut a building's cooling load by 70 percent.
green-roof-air.caption: Planted roof of Chicago City Hall in the United States, seen from above, photographed on 8 July 2008.
green-roof-air.credit: Photo: TonyTheTiger, via Wikimedia Commons, licence Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0. Resized.
sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency: Using Green Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands

green-roof-surface.name: Green roofs, roof surface
green-roof-surface.hook: The surface of a green roof can be 31 °C, or 56 °F, cooler than the surface of a conventional roof.
green-roof-surface.detail: This is the largest difference on this scale, because it compares the roof surface itself, where a dark roof in full sun gets hottest. Light roofs with shallow soil and hardy plants need little care. Deeper roofs with shrubs and trees need a stronger structure and regular upkeep.
green-roof-surface.caption: Planted roof of Chicago City Hall in the United States, seen from above, photographed on 8 July 2008.
green-roof-surface.credit: Photo: TonyTheTiger, via Wikimedia Commons, licence Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0. Resized.
sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency: Using Green Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands
